# Full breasts

Around the third or fourth day after you give birth, your breasts start to produce lots of milk. This is known as your milk 'coming in'.

## When your milk first comes in

- Your breasts may feel warm and look pink but not reddened.
- Your nipple and the dark area around it (areola) may feel firm, and it may take a little time for your baby to attach to feed.
- Your baby may not take all your milk during feeds. Watch and listen for your baby swallowing during a feed.
- If you still feel too full after a feed, express a little milk to feel more comfortable.
- Some babies can be unsettled during this time. It's OK to feed them often.
- Your baby might have lots of loose, green-coloured bowel motions (poo).

All of this is normal.

## Breastfeeding when your breasts feel full

- Hand express just before a feed to help soften your areola and move extra fluid that collects near your nipple in the first few days. This makes it easier for your baby to attach.
- Gently stroke your breasts to help your milk flow. Some people use a gentle warm pack to help milk flow, but cool packs after feeds usually work best.
- Offer your second breast to your baby after they finish feeding from the first.
- If your baby has fed from only one breast and the other feels uncomfortably full, try to express a little milk for comfort. Start the next feed with this breast.
- Swap breasts (left or right) each time you begin a new feed.

## Between feeds

- If your breasts feel too full, offer your baby another feed or express a little milk until they feel softer.
- Put a cold pack on your breasts for a few minutes after breastfeeding. This helps you feel more comfortable and reduces any swelling (inflammation). This is normal.
- Some people find that a supportive but not too tight bra feels comfortable, while others prefer not to wear one.
- You can take ibuprofen or paracetamol for pain relief. Follow the instructions on the packet.

Full breasts usually settle down quickly. If you're concerned, feel unwell, or if your breast is red and painful, get medical advice.

title: Low milk supply
body:
# Low milk supply

Low breastmilk supply is when your body is not making enough breastmilk for your baby’s needs.

You might worry about your milk supply, especially in the early stages of breastfeeding. Some people might stop breastfeeding because they think they don’t have enough milk. But most of the time your body is making enough milk for your baby.

If you have low milk supply it is usually for a short time. You can get help to improve your supply. You can talk to:

- your maternal and child health nurse
- a lactation consultant
- the Australian Breastfeeding Association
- your local doctor

## Common reasons you might think your milk supply is low

### “My baby feeds too often”

Breastfeeding your baby often helps your milk supply. Babies usually feed about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours.

When you start to breastfeed your baby might be unsettled, but this does not always mean you have low milk supply.

You can read our factsheet about starting to breastfeed: Breastfeeding: Getting started.

### “My breasts are feeling softer now”

Your breasts might start feeling softer and not as full after 3 to 12 weeks. Your milk supply changes to meet your baby’s needs.

If your baby keeps feeding well, your breasts should make enough milk.

### “My baby has suddenly started to feed more frequently”

Your baby might feed more when they want some more milk or are having a growth spurt.

When your baby feeds more over a couple of days your body will start to make more milk.

### “My baby only feeds for a short time”

After two or three months your baby will start to feed more quickly. Your baby is probably still getting enough milk.

You don’t need to worry as long as your baby continues to grow. Talk to your Maternal and Child Health Nurse or doctor if you are worried.

## How do you know if your baby is getting enough milk?

When your baby is one week, they usually:

- wake for feeds by themselves
- settle between most feeds
- have at least 6 to 8 soaked nappies in 24 hours if you are using cloth nappies
- have at least 4 to 5 heavy nappies in 24 hours if you are using disposable nappies
- do a soft yellow stool or poo at least once a day

After your baby is two weeks old they should be back to their birth weight. They will start gaining about 150 grams or more every week for the first three months.

## Why might you have low milk supply?

If you have low milk supply it may be because your baby:

- is not attaching well to your breast for feeding. This can also cause nipple pain and damage
- does not feed often enough. Babies usually feed about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours
- is not feeding effectively at your breast

You might have low milk supply because of other changes:

- you started using infant formula instead of breastfeeding
- you recently had mastitis

You might have low milk supply because you smoke cigarettes.

Some medicine can change your milk supply:

- contraception pills that have oestrogen in them
- over-the-counter and herbal medicine, like cold and flu tablets

## How can you help your milk supply?

You can help increase your milk supply with frequent feeding and expressing your breasts.

When you are breastfeeding or expressing, you can compress or massage your breasts to help your milk flow.

### Hold your baby skin-to-skin

You can hold your baby skin-to-skin when you are feeding. This is when your baby is only wearing a nappy so there is direct skin contact between you and your baby.

Skin-to-skin will help:

- keep your baby awake
- your body release hormones that help make breastmilk

### Feeding

You should breastfeed frequently, about every 2 or 3 hours. This means you will feed your baby 8 to 12 times in 24 hours.

You might need to wake and encourage your baby for some feeds.

Sometimes when you are feeding you could offer each breast twice to your baby. This is sometimes called ‘switch feeding’.

When your baby is getting tired or not swallowing as much, take your baby off that breast and switch to the other breast. Then switch again until your baby has had a feed from each breast twice.

This helps your baby get more milk from your breast more efficiently. This will not be something that you will do for a long time, just while you are getting your milk supply up.

Make sure your baby is attaching to your breast the best they can and that your baby is both sucking and swallowing, not just falling asleep while at your breast.

You can ask for help with this.

### Expressing

If your baby is sleepy at the breast and not feeding well, you might need to stop that feed and express from each breast twice instead.

For example, you could express for five minutes on the left side, five minutes on the right side and then do them both again.

Then use your expressed breastmilk to feed your baby.

You can express after breastfeeding some or most of the time. This helps to stimulate your breasts and make sure your breasts are well drained. This helps increase your milk supply.

Often it takes about one hour to feed and express. Then you and your baby can rest between feeds.

## Infant formula

If you need to give your baby extra milk, you should use your expressed breastmilk separately and always before any infant formula.

Get advice from a lactation consultant or other health professional before using infant formula.

## Medicine

Some people might use prescription medicine to help increase milk supply.

Talk to your doctor about whether medicine will help you.

## You might not be able to get a full breastmilk supply

Not everyone can get a full breastmilk supply.

You might have:

- a hormonal or medical condition
- had a premature baby
- unusual breast shape
- had breast surgery, like a breast reduction

If you think something is affecting your milk supply, talk to your doctor, midwife or lactation consultant. They can help you work out the best way to feed your baby.

Even if you cannot get a full milk supply, any breastmilk you give your baby is important.

## Who can you ask for help?

You can ask for help with feeding and expressing. You can ask:

- a lactation consultant
- your maternal and child health nurse
- another health care professional who understands breastfeeding

## Family Violence Support

### 1800 Respect National Helpline

Support for people impacted by sexual assault, domestic or family violence and abuse.

You can call any time of day or night.

1800 737 732

1800respect.org.au

## Do you need an interpreter?

If you need an interpreter, you can ask for one.

## For more information

### Victorian Maternal & Child Health Line

You can call any time of day or night.

13 22 29

### Australian Breastfeeding Association Breastfeeding Helpline

1800 686 268

breastfeeding.asn.au

You can find breastfeeding information and factsheets on our website:

thewomens.org.au/health-information/breastfeeding

title: Infant formula
body:
# Infant formula

## Key points

- Baby formula is the only safe alternative to breastmilk until babies are 12 months old.
- All Australian cow's milk-based formulas meet strict standards and have all the nutrients babies need for healthy growth and development.
- Babies who can't have cow's milk-based formula might need special formula. Use these formulas only under medical supervision.

## What is infant or baby formula?

Most baby formula is made from cow's milk that has been modified so that it suits babies' nutritional needs. It's not the same as cow's milk.

## Why babies need formula rather than cow's milk

All baby formula has added vitamins, minerals and fats that babies need, which they can't get from normal cow's milk.

Also, babies can't digest and absorb cow's milk as completely or easily as breastmilk or formula. That's because the protein level in cow's milk is too high for babies.

For these reasons, you shouldn't give cow's milk to your baby as their main milk drink until your baby is over 12 months old.

## Stage 1 and stage 2 formulas

Cow's milk-based baby formulas for babies up to 6 months of age are called stage 1 or starter formulas. You can use stage 1 formulas from 0-12 months old.

From 6 months, you can choose stage 2 or follow-on formula, but you don't need to change to stage 2. These formulas aren't better for your baby than starter or stage 1 formulas.

## Which baby formula is best?

Every baby formula you can buy in Australia meets strict Australian Standards.

All cow's milk-based baby formulas are safe and have all the nutrients babies need for healthy growth and development. All these formulas suit most babies.

Some brands have extra ingredients added to them and are more expensive, but you don't need to buy those brands for your baby. A hospital's use of a particular brand of infant formula doesn't mean that the brand is the 'best'.

For most healthy full-term babies who are having infant formula, cow's milk-based baby formulas are recommended until 12 months of age.

If you're thinking of feeding your baby something other than breastmilk or cow's milk-based formula, talk to your paediatrician, GP or child and family health nurse first.

You can buy baby formula in powder form or 'ready to drink' form. Either is fine for your baby, but 'ready to drink' is usually more expensive.

## Baby formula with special additives

Some baby formulas have extra ingredients added to them to make them more like breastmilk. But these ingredients don't necessarily work in the same way as breastmilk in your baby's body.

Some breastmilk ingredients added to baby formulas include:

- LCPs (long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids)
- betacarotene
- prebiotics
- probiotics

## Special baby formulas

For babies under 12 months of age, cow's milk-based baby formula is recommended over formulas made from soybeans or goat's milk. It's also recommended over lactose-free formula.

Babies who can't have cow's milk-based formula might need special formula. You should use special baby formulas only under medical supervision.

### Soy-based baby formula

Some babies can't have dairy-based products because of allergies or intolerances. Or you might not want to use regular baby formula because of cultural, religious or other beliefs.

Soy formulas are considered safe to use if your baby needs them.

Soy-based formulas don't prevent or reduce the risk of your child developing allergies.

### Hydrolysed baby formula

Hydrolysed formula is cow's milk-based formula in which the milk proteins have been broken down into smaller components.

- Partially hydrolysed formula is also called 'HA' or hypoallergenic formula. These formulas aren't suitable if your baby has a cow's milk protein allergy.
- Extensively hydrolysed formula has protein that is broken down even more. If your baby has a diagnosed cow's milk protein allergy and you aren't breastfeeding, your doctor might recommend an extensively hydrolysed infant formula.

There's no evidence that giving babies hydrolysed infant formula prevents allergy problems from developing, even if you have a family history of allergies.

### Prethickened formula and thickening agents

Prethickened, also called 'AR' or anti-reflux, formula is cow's milk-based formula that has a thickener added.

You can also buy thickening agents to add to standard baby formula yourself.

Your GP might recommend thickeners or prethickened formula if you're using formula and your baby has gastro-oesophageal reflux.

You should use prethickened formula or thickeners only in consultation with your doctor.

## Homemade baby formula

Homemade baby formulas that use bone broth, 'raw' milk, or skim, evaporated, powdered or sweetened condensed milk aren't suitable alternatives to breastmilk or shop-bought cow's milk-based baby formula.

Homemade baby formula can contain many ingredients that aren't safe for your baby. Also, it generally won't have the correct amounts of the essential nutrients that your baby needs.

## Changing baby formula

Once you've settled on a baby formula for your baby, it's best not to change formula unless you need to.

It can take several days for babies to adjust to new formula.

Also, different formulas have different-sized scoops and are made up in different ways, so it can be confusing if you change formulas.

If you do change formula, read the directions on the new formula label carefully.

If you think your baby needs a different formula, it's a good idea to talk with your GP or child and family health nurse.

## Toddler formulas

Your baby doesn't need formula after 12 months.

This includes toddler or stage 3 formulas. At this age, toddlers should be getting most of their nutrition from solid food and can have cow's milk as a drink.

If toddlers are having toddler formula, it can reduce their appetite for food. This can mean they don't get the nutrients they need. It can also contribute to fussy eating.

You can read more about how to make, store and transport formula, how to bottle-feed, and how to sterilise bottle-feeding equipment.

When your baby is around 6 months old, you can start helping your child learn to drink from a cup. You can aim to wean your baby off the bottle by the time they turn 12 months old.

title: Bottle-feeding babies: giving the bottle
body:
# Bottle-feeding babies: giving the bottle

## Key points

- Test the flow of formula or breastmilk before bottle-feeding.
- Hold your baby close on a slight incline and keep the bottle at an angle.
- Let your baby decide when they’ve had enough to drink.
- Avoid leaving your baby unattended or putting your baby to bed with a bottle.

## About bottle-feeding

If your baby can’t always feed directly from the breast, you might choose to bottle-feed with expressed breastmilk.

Or you might need to feed your baby infant formula, which is the only safe alternative to breastmilk.

Before you bottle-feed your baby, it’s important to know how to clean and sterilise bottle-feeding equipment, as well as how to prepare, store and warm bottles of formula. This will help to keep your baby safe from infection and make sure your baby is getting the right nutrition.

## Getting the right flow when bottle-feeding

To test the flow of the formula or breastmilk, hold the bottle upside down when it’s filled with liquid at room temperature.

The liquid should drip steadily from the teat but not pour out.

If you have to shake the bottle vigorously to see the drip, the flow is too slow. Your baby might go to sleep before drinking what they need.

When you feed your baby, you might see a little leakage at the corners of your baby’s mouth. This doesn’t mean the flow is too fast. It’s nothing to worry about. It will stop as your baby gets older.

If your baby is having trouble getting formula or breastmilk from the bottle, try a faster teat.

If your baby doesn’t seem to be swallowing quickly enough, try a slower teat.

You might need to try a few different teats before you find one that suits.

## Giving your baby the bottle

Make yourself comfortable.

Cuddle your baby close to you, holding them gently but firmly and on a slight incline.

Put the teat against your baby’s lips. Your baby will open their mouth and start to suck.

Keep the neck of the bottle at an angle so that it’s filled with formula or breastmilk and so that small air bubbles can rise through the milk as your baby drinks.

This will help to reduce the amount of air your baby swallows and might help with burping.

If you don’t see air bubbles rising, try loosening the ring a little.

When your baby stops sucking strongly or when about half of the formula or breastmilk has gone, gently remove the bottle and see whether your baby wants to burp.

Once you’ve tried burping your baby, you can offer the bottle again.

Holding, cuddling and talking to your baby during feeding will help your baby develop and grow. Feeding is also a great opportunity to bond with your baby.

## Paced bottle-feeding

Babies who are normally breastfed might find it hard to pace themselves when bottle-feeding, particularly if they’re premature.

This is because they’re used to controlling the flow of breastmilk. Sometimes these babies can drink too much too quickly.

Paced feeding can sometimes help.

This involves holding your baby in an upright position and letting them rest every few minutes.

If you’re interested in paced bottle-feeding, it’s best to get help from your child and family health nurse or a lactation consultant.

## When your baby doesn’t finish the bottle or goes to sleep while feeding

Don’t worry if your baby doesn’t finish the bottle.

Babies are very good at judging how much they need, so you can let your baby decide when they’ve had enough formula or breastmilk.

If your baby goes to sleep during a feed, put your baby over your shoulder, rub their back, and stroke their head, legs and tummy. This can help your baby to wake up.

A nappy change is a good way to wake up your baby if that doesn’t work.

Wait until your baby is properly awake before offering the rest of the formula or breastmilk.

If your baby doesn’t finish all the formula or breastmilk, throw it away within one hour.

When your baby drinks from the bottle, bacteria from your baby’s mouth get into the milk. These bacteria can make your baby sick if you give your baby the same bottle again later.

## When your baby refuses the bottle

Babies sometimes refuse a bottle altogether.

Here are things to try if this happens:

- Try a new feeding position or change the feeding environment. For example, move around while you’re feeding, find a quieter place to feed, or play some relaxing background music.
- Try again later when your baby is more settled. For example, give your baby a bath and then try again.
- Ask your partner or another family member to give the bottle to your baby. This can help if you usually breastfeed your baby.
- Check the flow of formula or breastmilk. If the flow is too slow, this can frustrate your baby. You might need to try a different teat.
- Let your baby open their mouth for the bottle when they’re ready, rather than putting the teat into their mouth.
- Offer the formula or breastmilk from a small cup or spoon. To do this, sit your baby up and offer them small sips.

If your baby is regularly refusing the bottle, speak to your child and family health nurse for advice.

If you think your baby is refusing the bottle because they’re unwell, treat your baby’s symptoms or take your baby to see your GP.

## How much do bottle-feeding babies drink?

Newborn babies commonly have 6 to 8 feeds every 24 hours, but there’s no set amount of food or number of feeds your baby should have.

Different babies drink different amounts of formula or breastmilk.

Some might have feeds close together and others further apart. Some babies have predictable feeding patterns, whereas other babies change their feeding times each day.

Feed your baby whenever they’re hungry.

You’ll see baby cues that say ‘I’m hungry’ — for example, your baby will make sucking noises or start turning towards the breast or bottle.

If your baby stops sucking or turns their head away from the bottle, you’ll know they’ve had enough.

As your baby eats more and more solid food, the total amount of breastmilk or formula they take in a day will decrease.

The amount of breastmilk or formula will also decrease as your baby starts to drink from a cup instead of a bottle.

Some babies never drink the ‘recommended amount’ for their age and size, and others need more.

Plenty of wet nappies, consistent weight gain, and a thriving, active baby mean all is well.

If you’re concerned about how much breastmilk or formula your baby is taking, talk to your child and family health nurse or GP.

## Bottle-feeding in bed: risks

Bottle-feeding in bed has several risks for your baby.

It’s important to put your baby to bed without a bottle or to take the bottle away after your baby has finished feeding.

### Choking and chest infections

Babies who fall asleep flat on their back while bottle-feeding can draw liquid into their lungs.

They might then choke on it or get a chest infection.

### Ear infections

If your baby drinks while lying flat, milk can flow into the ear cavity, which can cause ear infections.

### Tooth decay

Bottle-feeding in bed can increase your baby’s risk of tooth decay.

This is because there’s less saliva in children’s mouths during sleep, and saliva protects teeth from the sugar in milk.

### Sleep associations

If your baby gets used to falling asleep with a bottle in bed, they might depend on it to get to sleep.

This can make it more difficult for your baby to settle for sleep independently.

## Prop feeding

Prop feeding is risky and isn’t recommended.

Prop feeding is using a rolled-up blanket, pillow or other prop to keep the bottle in the baby’s mouth.

Prop feeding can increase the risk of choking, suffocation, ear infections and tooth decay.

## Using a feeding cup

When your baby is around 6 months old, you can help your baby start learning to drink from a cup.

It’s best to wean your baby off the bottle by the time your baby is 12 months old.

It’s important to continue to thoroughly wash and sterilise feeding cups containing infant formula or breastmilk until your baby is 12 months old.

title: Preparing bottles for infant formula (in pictures)
body:
# Preparing bottles for infant formula (in pictures)

## Clean equipment

- Wipe down the preparation area.
- Wash your hands with soap and water.
- Wash all equipment in hot soapy water, including:
  - bottles
  - teats
  - discs
  - caps
  - rings
- Use a bottle brush.
- Rinse everything thoroughly.
- Squirt water through the holes in the teats.

## Sterilise equipment

- Cover all equipment with water and bring it to the boil.
- Boil for 5 minutes.

Or use:

- a microwave steriliser
- a steam steriliser
- a chemical steriliser

Follow the manufacturer's instructions.

Store empty sterilised bottles in a clean container in the refrigerator.

## Safety

- Keep children away from boiling water.
- Let equipment cool in the pot until it is safe to touch.
- Use sterilised equipment within 24 hours.

## Making infant formula

- Boil fresh tap water.
- Allow it to cool for at least 30 minutes until lukewarm (about body temperature).
- Prepare only one bottle at a time.
- If needed, store sterilised sealed bottles filled with cooled boiled water in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours.
- Read the formula tin instructions for the correct amount of water.
- Add the cooled boiled water to a sterilised bottle.

## Add the formula

- Check the tin for the correct number of scoops.
- Tap the scoop lightly.
- Level the powder with a sterilised knife.
- Add the powder to the cooled boiled water.

## Prepare the bottle

- Put the cap or disc on the bottle.
- Shake well until the powder has dissolved.
- Use prepared formula within one hour.
- Throw away any leftover formula.

## Warming the bottle

- Warm the bottle in a container of warm water for no longer than 10 minutes.
- Shake the bottle.
- Test a drop on your wrist.
- Check that milk flows freely through the teat.

Cold formula is also safe to use.

## Preparing bottles when going out

- Fill the bottle with the correct amount of cooled boiled water.
- Keep it in an insulated bag with a cool pack.
- Carry the measured formula powder separately.
- Mix the formula only when your baby is ready for a feed.

title: Six safe sleep recommendations
body:
# Six safe sleep recommendations

Red Nose recommends six key steps to reduce the risk of sudden infant death, for all babies from birth to 1 year.

Our Safe Sleep recommendations are based on research and are shown to reduce the risk to your baby whilst they are sleeping. Following them for every sleep will help keep your baby safe.

## 1. Always place baby on their back to sleep

Placing baby on their back to sleep helps keep their airway clear and ensures their protective reflexes work.

Back sleeping reduces the risk of suffocation, overheating and choking.

## 2. Keep baby’s head and face uncovered

Babies control their temperature through their face and head, so keeping baby’s face and head uncovered during sleep helps reduce the risk of overheating.

It also helps keep their airways clear which reduces the risk of suffocation.

## 3. Keep baby smoke free, before and after birth

Smoking during pregnancy and around baby once they are born increases the risk of sudden infant death – this includes second-hand smoke.

If you or your partner smoke, don’t smoke around baby and never smoke where baby sleeps.

For free help to quit smoking, call Quitline on 13 78 48.

## 4. Provide a safe sleeping environment, night and day

The safest place for baby to sleep is in their own safe space, with a safe mattress and safe bedding.

Baby should always be placed on their back to sleep, with their feet at the bottom of the bassinet or cot.

### Choose a safe cot

Choose a safe cot which meets Australian Standard AS/NZS 2172:2003.

### Choose a safe mattress

Choose a safe mattress which is:

- firm
- flat
- the right size for your safe cot
- compliant with voluntary Australian Standard AS/NZS 8811.1:2013

### Choose safe bedding

Choose safe bedding which is:

- lightweight
- firmly tucked in
- only pulled up to the chest

### If using a sleeping bag

Choose a safe sleeping bag which is:

- well fitted across the neck and chest
- used with baby’s arms out
- without a hood

### Keep soft and bulky items out of the sleep space

Do not use soft items in the cot.

Soft items in the sleep space are dangerous and increase the risk of suffocation and overheating.

This includes:

- doonas or loose blankets
- pillows
- cot bumpers
- lambs wool
- soft toys such as a teddy or comforter

## 5. Sleep baby in their own safe sleep space in the same room as their parent or caregiver for at least the first 6 months

The safest place for baby to sleep is in their own safe space, in the same room as their parent or adult caregiver for at least the first 6 months.

## 6. Breastfeed baby, if possible

Breastfeeding has been shown to reduce the risk of sudden infant death.

## Further support

If you would like advice on how to safely sleep your baby, call the Red Nose Safe Sleep Advice Line on 1300 998 698.

The advice line is available between 9 am and 5 pm Monday to Friday (AEST).

## Co-sleeping

Red Nose does not recommend co-sleeping as there is evidence that co-sleeping may lead to unsafe sleeping practices.

However, some families choose to co-sleep or find that it happens accidentally. Red Nose provides information on how to co-sleep in a way that best reduces risk.

Last updated: 6 August 2025

title: Safe sleep environments for babies
body:
# Safe sleep environments for babies

## Key points

- Safe sleep environments protect baby airways during sleep and make it easier for babies to breathe.
- In a safe sleep environment, your baby sleeps on their back, on a firm, flat and level surface, in a space that’s clear, not too hot and smoke free.
- Check your baby’s sleep environment at home, child care and any other place your baby sleeps.

## What is a safe sleep environment for your baby?

Wherever and whenever your baby sleeps, they must be able to breathe easily.

A safe sleep environment helps to keep your baby’s airways open and reduces the risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI), including SIDS and fatal sleep accidents.

A safe sleep environment for your baby involves a:

- safe sleep surface
- safe sleep space
- safe sleep position
- safe sleep location

## Safe sleep surface: firm, flat and level

### What is a sleep surface?

A sleep surface is what your baby sleeps on or in.

### What is a safe sleep surface for your baby?

For a sleep surface to be safe, it must be firm, flat and level.

A firm, flat and level surface might be on a mattress in a cot or portacot, bassinet, baby box, pepi-pod or co-sleeper that meets the Australian Consumer Goods (Infant Sleep Products) Safety Standard 2024.

You might also be able to create a safe sleep surface while co-sleeping.

A safe sleep surface has safe bedding.

This includes a tight-fitting fitted sheet over a well-fitted waterproof mattress protector.

The mattress protector shouldn’t be padded or soft.

This makes it more likely that your child will be able to breathe easily, even if they roll over.

### What is an unsafe sleep surface for your baby?

An unsafe sleep surface is soft, curved, inclined, uneven or unstable.

Unsafe sleep surfaces include:

- sheepskin or lamb’s wool underlays
- couches, with or without someone else
- makeshift bedding
- pillows
- beanbags
- waterbeds
- prams
- slings
- swings
- bouncers
- child car seats

Child car seats protect your baby from injury in car crashes, but sleeping on an incline can make it harder for your baby to breathe easily.

It’s best to check your baby’s breathing and take regular breaks during long drives.

## Safe sleep space: clear, not too hot and smoke free

### What is a sleep space?

Your baby’s sleep space is what’s around your baby while they’re sleeping.

### What is a safe sleep space for your baby?

A safe sleep space is clear of anything that might stop your baby from breathing easily, including things that pose strangulation or suffocation risks.

For example:

- Your baby’s face and head are uncovered.
- There are no doonas, pillows, nests, loungers, cot bumpers, mattress padding, soft toys or sleep positioners around your baby.
- Your baby’s coverings are lightweight and tucked in securely at your baby’s chest level with their feet positioned at the bottom of the cot.
- Or your baby is using a safe infant sleeping bag or suit instead of coverings.
- There are no teething necklaces, dummy chains and so on attached to your baby.

A safe sleep space also protects your baby from overheating.

For example:

- Your baby is dressed in clothing that’s warm but not hot.
- Your baby isn’t wearing a beanie or hat.
- The room is neither too hot nor too cold.
- If you’re using heating or cooling, it should be set to a moderate temperature and directed away from your baby.
- There are no electric blankets or hot water bottles.

There should also be clear space around your baby.

If your baby is in a cot or portacot, there should be a 30-cm clear space around it, with no items that your baby can reach, like plastic, blind cords, mosquito nets and electrical cords.

If you’re co-sleeping, consider whether the sleep space is big enough. It needs to fit everyone who sleeps there, with room for a clear space around your baby.

There are many cots and other products on the market. Many make claims about protecting babies against SUDI.

But a cot, portacot, bassinet, baby box, pepi-pod or co-sleeper that meets the Australian Consumer Goods (Infant Sleep Products) Safety Standard 2024 is the safest place for your baby to sleep, provided that it’s well-maintained and clean and has a well-fitting, firm mattress and safe bedding.

## Safe sleep position: baby on their back

### What is a sleep position?

A sleep position is how your baby sleeps.

### What is a safe sleep position for your baby?

The safest sleep position for your baby is on their back.

This is for several reasons:

- The reflexes that keep your baby’s airways open work better when your baby is on their back.
- These reflexes include swallowing, stirring and waking up if their airways become blocked.
- Your baby is less likely to rebreathe air they’ve just breathed out.
- Rebreathed air contains less oxygen.
- Your baby has plenty of space around their mouth and nose, so their airways are more likely to stay open.

At 3 to 4 months, many babies start showing signs that they can roll onto their tummies.

When this happens for your baby, it’s time to stop wrapping.

Your baby needs their arms free so they can push up to lift their head.

Once your baby can roll easily onto their tummy and back again, at 4 to 6 months, keep putting your baby to sleep on their back, but let your baby find their own sleeping position.

## Safe sleep location: sharing parent’s room

It’s safest for your baby to share a room with you for the first year of life or at least the first 6 months.

The reflexes that keep your baby’s airways open work better when they’re close to you while they’re sleeping.

## Keep your baby’s environment smoke and vapour free

Keep your baby’s environment smoke and vapour free before and after birth.

The link between SUDI and smoking or vaping is strong, even when parents smoke away from their babies.

If you want to quit smoking or vaping and you’re finding it hard, call Quitline on 137 848.

You could also speak to your GP or child and family health nurse.

## Safe sleep away from home

It’s best not to assume that other people know about safe sleep practices, even professional child carers.

It’s a good idea to share safe sleep information with carers.

It’s also important to check the sleep environment at your baby’s child care setting or any other place your baby will be spending time, and make sure that the sleep surface, space and position are safe for your baby.

## Breastfeeding and safe sleep

Breastfeeding reduces the risk of SUDI, including SIDS and fatal sleeping accidents.

Regardless of whether your baby is breastfed or bottle-fed, it’s still very important to create a safe sleep environment that helps your baby breathe easily.

Last updated or reviewed: 8 April 2026

title: Jaundice and your newborn baby
body:
# Jaundice and your newborn baby

Newborn babies often appear to have a yellowish tinge to their skin. This is called jaundice.

Jaundice occurs when a chemical called bilirubin builds up in the baby’s blood and tissues.

In most babies jaundice is a normal event and is not serious. It nearly always disappears within a few days, without the need for any treatment.

## Why is jaundice common in newborn babies?

Bilirubin is a yellow-red pigment that is released when the body’s red blood cells are broken down, a normal process that happens in all of us.

It is normal to find small amounts of bilirubin in everyone’s blood and a newborn baby’s blood usually has more.

Bilirubin is removed from the blood by the liver.

Most babies will develop some jaundice in the first few days of life because:

- while you are pregnant, your baby’s bilirubin is removed by the placenta and by your liver. After the birth, your baby’s liver has to take over the job of removing the bilirubin and this can take a little while
- newborn babies have extra red blood cells that are broken down after birth, so more bilirubin is produced

## How do I know if my baby is jaundiced?

If your baby is jaundiced their skin will appear to be yellow.

You will typically notice it three to five days after birth.

It is best seen in good daylight.

Jaundice can usually be seen in the face, then as the bilirubin levels in the blood increase it becomes visible on the chest, abdomen, arms and legs.

Jaundice can be harder to see in babies with darker skin.

## Is jaundice harmful to my baby?

Most jaundice is mild and will not harm your baby.

It will usually disappear as their liver matures towards the end of the first week of life. This is called physiological jaundice.

Sometimes the bilirubin level is high enough to need treatment, as very high bilirubin levels can affect the brain and in rare, extreme cases can cause brain damage.

This is not the usual case for jaundice.

Babies who develop very high levels of jaundice have an underlying problem that causes the bilirubin levels to get so high. This is called pathological jaundice.

Pathological jaundice is why both health care workers and families need to check jaundice.

It is always important to watch the baby and monitor the level of bilirubin in the blood and, if necessary, treat the jaundice promptly.

## How will I know if my baby’s jaundice level is very high?

All babies born at the Women’s have their bilirubin level checked with a skin sensor after 48 hours of age, at the same time as their routine heel prick for the Newborn Screening Test (NST), and at any other time there is a concern about jaundice.

If this skin test suggests a high bilirubin level, then a heel prick blood test is required. This gives a more exact level of bilirubin in the blood.

Most babies with jaundice will not need any treatment.

However, once the bilirubin on the blood test reaches a certain level, treatment with blue lights (phototherapy) will be recommended.

The bilirubin level at which treatment is recommended is still much lower than the level which could harm your baby.

## When should I worry about my baby’s jaundice?

Your midwife will monitor your baby for jaundice while you are both in hospital.

After discharge from hospital your baby will be checked by visiting midwife, nurse or your independent midwife.

Your local Maternal and Child Health nurse and family doctor will also provide you with support and observe your baby.

Your baby’s jaundice needs to be checked by a doctor at the hospital if they:

- look yellow and are less than 48 hours of age — take your baby immediately to the Emergency Department at the hospital
- are rapidly becoming more yellow
- are yellow on the tummy, arms or legs
- are too sleepy to feed
- are feeding poorly
- have fewer wet or dirty nappies
- have a combination of the above, or if your baby seems unwell

In hospital, the doctor will ask you questions about your baby’s feeding, sleepiness and about the number of wet and dirty nappies.

Your baby will be weighed, examined and a decision will be made about the need to measure and treat the bilirubin level, and whether any other tests are needed.

## How is jaundice treated?

If needed, jaundice is treated by exposing the baby’s skin to blue light. This is called phototherapy.

The blue light helps to break down the bilirubin in the skin until the baby’s liver takes over.

During phototherapy your baby will be swaddled in a flexible blue-light wrap, wearing only a nappy and with a blanket over the top of the blue light if needed.

Your baby can be held and fed as normal during phototherapy.

The blue-light wrap only needs to be taken off during nappy changes and bath time.

Phototherapy is very safe, but can cause your baby to have a mild skin rash or loose bowel movements.

The treatment is usually only needed for 2 to 3 days.

During phototherapy your baby will need a blood test every day.

Babies with very high jaundice levels are sometimes admitted to the Newborn Intensive Care unit for more intense phototherapy.

In severe cases of pathological jaundice the baby may need to have new blood transfused and the old blood removed. This is called an exchange transfusion.

This is rarely needed and we would give you full information about this procedure if your baby requires it.

title: Umbilical and baby belly button care
body:
# Umbilical and baby belly button care

## Key points

- The baby belly button is what’s left of the umbilical cord after birth.
- Keep the umbilical stump clean and dry. It will fall off on its own.
- See your GP if you notice a red or discoloured lump, bulging or swelling around the belly button after the umbilical stump has fallen off.

## Your baby’s umbilical stump and belly button: what to expect

After your baby’s birth, the umbilical cord is clamped and cut.

The part of the umbilical cord that’s still attached to your baby is the umbilical stump. Often the clamp is still attached to the stump.

During the first few days after birth, the stump gets darker, shrivels and eventually falls off with the clamp.

What’s left is your baby’s belly button.

Sometimes this takes 1 to 2 weeks.

While the stump is drying up and just after it falls off, you might notice some oozing around your baby’s belly button.

This might be clear, sticky or brownish, and it might leave a mark on your baby’s clothes or nappy.

It might also smell a little bit. This is part of the healing process.

## When to be concerned about your baby’s umbilical stump or belly button

You should take your baby to see your GP or child and family health nurse if the stump hasn’t fallen off after more than 2 weeks.

Also see your GP or nurse if the area around the stump:

- is red or discoloured
- has a bad smell
- is warm and tender to touch

See your GP as soon as possible if:

- you’re still seeing sticky liquid several days after the stump has fallen off
- your baby’s belly button area gets hot, red, discoloured or swollen
- your baby is lethargic or otherwise unwell

If your baby has a fever, take them to a hospital emergency department.

## How to clean and care for the umbilical stump and belly button

You can gently wash your baby’s umbilical stump and belly button area during bath time or if the area gets wee or poo on it.

### Cleaning the umbilical stump

Always wash your hands before cleaning the umbilical stump.

Use water and a clean, soft washcloth or cotton ball to clean the stump.

It’s OK to use a mild baby cleanser.

Don’t use antiseptic, alcohol wipes or creams.

After cleaning, gently pat the area around the stump dry with a clean, soft towel or cloth.

### Caring for the stump and belly button

If your baby’s nappy covers the stump, fold the top of the nappy down and away from the stump.

This will allow it to air dry.

Never try to pull the stump off yourself, even if it looks like it’s ready to fall off.

After the stump has fallen off, keep the area clean and dry until it heals completely.

## What is umbilical granuloma?

After the umbilical stump has fallen off, some babies can develop a small pink, red or discoloured lump in the belly button area.

This is called an umbilical granuloma.

Sometimes the lump might ooze a small amount of yellow or clear fluid.

Keep the area clean and dry.

An umbilical granuloma might get better on its own, but it’s good to have your GP or child and family nurse look at the lump.

## What is an umbilical hernia?

If your baby develops a bulge or swelling near the belly button, it might be an umbilical hernia.

An umbilical hernia is often more noticeable when your baby cries or strains to do a poo.

This usually isn’t dangerous, and it doesn’t hurt your baby.

An umbilical hernia will often go away between the ages of 3 and 5 years.

It’s good to have your GP or child and family health nurse look at the bulge.

Last updated or reviewed: 17 February 2026

title: Australian Postnatal Care Guidelines
body:
# Australian Postnatal Care Guidelines

Australian Living Evidence Collaboration

Version 7, published 19 June 2025

---

## Secondary postpartum haemorrhage

Heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum haemorrhage, PPH) occurs in 5–15% of births in Australia.

Primary postpartum haemorrhage occurs during or within 24 hours after birth.

Secondary postpartum haemorrhage refers to bleeding that occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after birth.

Most cases of secondary postpartum haemorrhage occur in women with no identifiable risk factors.

### Information for all women

Within 24 hours of birth, discuss:

- what vaginal bleeding after birth (lochia) is
- what vaginal bleeding is expected after birth
- the expected timeframe for lochia

### Advise women to seek immediate medical advice if:

- vaginal bleeding is sudden or very heavy (for example, soaking more than one sanitary pad every 1–2 hours)
- lochia continues beyond the expected timeframe or increases beyond normal fluctuation
- blood loss includes large clots (larger than a plum), placental tissue or membranes
- the bleeding becomes brighter red again
- symptoms of infection develop, including abdominal, pelvic or perineal pain, dizziness, fatigue, fever, shivering, or unpleasant-smelling vaginal bleeding or discharge
- they are concerned about their vaginal bleeding after birth

### Good practice

Discuss secondary postpartum haemorrhage at each postnatal contact between 24 hours and 8 weeks after birth.

If secondary postpartum haemorrhage is identified, women should receive prompt assessment by an appropriate clinician, which may include emergency medical attention.

### Additional information

Women may not recognise the symptoms of secondary postpartum haemorrhage and may mistake them for normal postpartum bleeding.

Explain the difference between normal lochia and secondary postpartum haemorrhage, including symptoms of possible infection.

Lochia is the normal vaginal discharge after birth and usually lasts around 24–36 days, although it can continue for more than 6 weeks in some women.

The stages of lochia are:

#### Lochia rubra

- First 3–7 days
- Red or red-brown

#### Lochia serosa

- Typically the second week
- Brown or pink

#### Lochia alba

- From the second or third week until around the sixth week
- Whitish or yellowish-white

Provide this information both verbally and in writing within 24 hours of birth, and revisit it during follow-up appointments until 8 weeks postpartum.

Menstruation may also return during the postpartum period and should be discussed where appropriate.

## Social and emotional screening

Perinatal depression and anxiety are very common, affecting approximately one in every five mothers in Australia.

These recommendations are based on the Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period: Australian Clinical Practice Guideline from the Centre of Perinatal Excellence (COPE).

### Considerations before screening and assessment

Consider the administration of a screening tool as part of a multicomponent approach that must involve:

- clinical judgement
- clear protocols for further assessment of women who screen positive
- appropriate care pathways

Health professionals should seek training in:

- parent-centred communication skills
- psychosocial assessment
- culturally safe care
- trauma-informed care

When screening Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, and women from culturally diverse backgrounds including migrant and refugee women, consider the language and cultural appropriateness of screening tools.

Where possible, give Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women the option of screening or assessment by an Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander worker or professional.

With the woman's consent, include findings from depression or anxiety screening and psychosocial risk assessment in communication or handover to other health professionals involved in care.

### Screening for postnatal depression

Varying emotions are common during the postnatal period. Mental health screening and psychosocial assessment should be explained as tools that can help identify when further support may be useful.

Screening should be undertaken sensitively.

Important considerations include:

- building rapport
- promoting acceptability
- ensuring adequate follow-up and support
- considering whether other people should be present during the assessment
- providing non-judgmental and compassionate care

It may take more than one visit before a woman feels comfortable being screened or disclosing concerns.

Obtain informed consent before depression or anxiety screening and psychosocial assessment, including explaining the limits of confidentiality where there may be risks to the woman or baby.

Cultural background should be considered when screening for depression and anxiety.

For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, consider:

- rapport and trust
- language barriers
- cultural appropriateness of the screening tool
- possible concerns about the consequences of disclosing mental health concerns
- whether the woman would prefer screening by an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander worker or professional

For women from other culturally diverse backgrounds, including migrant and refugee women, use culturally appropriate and translated tools where available.

### Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale

Use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) to screen women for a possible depressive disorder.

Arrange further assessment for women with an EPDS score of 13 or more.

For women with an EPDS score between 10 and 12:

- monitor
- repeat the EPDS in 2–4 weeks

Repeat the EPDS at any time if clinically indicated.

For women from culturally diverse backgrounds, including migrant and refugee women, use appropriately translated versions of the EPDS with culturally relevant cut-off scores.

Consider using the Kimberley Mum’s Mood Scale (KMMS) as an alternative to the EPDS for screening for depression in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women.

### EPDS Question 10

For a woman with a positive score on Question 10 of the EPDS:

- undertake or arrange immediate further assessment
- if there is any disclosure of suicidal ideation, take urgent action in accordance with local protocol or policy

### Timing of postnatal depression screening

The guideline includes a consensus recommendation to conduct the first postnatal screening for depression 6–12 weeks after birth and plan to repeat it at least once later in the postnatal period.

**Recommendation status:** This is a draft recommendation approved by the LEAPP Steering Committee on 19 March 2024 and has not yet been approved by NHMRC.


---

### Screening for postnatal anxiety

Anxiety disorders are very common in the perinatal period and should be considered as part of the broader clinical assessment.

As part of the clinical assessment, use:

- anxiety items from the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), specifically items 3, 4 and 5
- or another validated tool that includes anxiety items
- and relevant items in structured psychosocial assessment tools

### Using the EPDS

The EPDS is widely used for depression screening in the postnatal period and can also contribute to assessment of anxiety.

The EPDS asks about mental health during the previous 7 days. Repeat assessment may be required depending on the woman’s circumstances.

The EPDS is a self-report tool. A printed copy should preferably be completed without consultation with others.

Where appropriate, a health professional may administer the questionnaire verbally during:

- a face-to-face consultation
- a telephone consultation
- a telehealth consultation

Some women may prefer electronic administration of the EPDS, followed by advice about any need for further assessment.

### Cultural considerations

For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, consider using the Kimberley Mum’s Mood Scale (KMMS), including items 3, 4 and 5, as an alternative to the EPDS for screening for anxiety.

If using the KMMS, use the tool in its entirety, including both Part 1 and Part 2.

Where an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander worker or professional is available, ask the woman whether she would prefer screening to be undertaken by that worker or professional.

For women from other cultural backgrounds, appropriately translated versions of the EPDS are available in multiple languages.

### Important considerations

A positive response to Question 10 of the EPDS, which relates to self-harm, should always be followed up regardless of the total EPDS score.

Very low total EPDS scores should also be discussed, as they may indicate reservations about disclosure.

## Assessing psychosocial risk factors that affect mental health

Psychosocial assessment focuses on current and past circumstances that may affect mental health and helps facilitate timely referral and care where appropriate.

These recommendations are based on the Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period: Australian Clinical Practice Guideline from the Centre of Perinatal Excellence (COPE).

### Recommended

Use the Antenatal Risk Questionnaire (ANRQ) to assess the presence of psychosocial risk factors.

### Consensus recommendations

Undertake psychosocial assessment together with a tool that screens for current symptoms of depression or anxiety, such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), at 6–12 weeks after birth.

Use appropriately translated versions of the ANRQ where available.

Consider the language and cultural appropriateness of any psychosocial assessment tool used.

Consider using the Kimberley Mum's Mood Scale (KMMS) instead of the ANRQ when assessing psychosocial risk factors in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women.

### Good practice

Seek training in:

- psychosocial assessment
- the use of psychosocial assessment tools

Ensure there are clear guidelines about:

- interpretation of assessment results
- thresholds for referral
- ongoing monitoring

Discuss with the woman:

- the psychosocial risk factors she has identified
- how these may affect her mental health
- what support is available

### Additional information

Psychosocial assessment identifies factors that may increase the risk of mental health difficulties and can occur alongside depression and anxiety screening to provide a more complete picture of wellbeing.

The Antenatal Risk Questionnaire (ANRQ):

- has been the recommended psychosocial assessment tool in Australia since 2017
- identifies risk factors including relationships, social support, significant life events and mental health history
- is not a diagnostic tool
- helps identify women who may benefit from further assessment or support

For the postnatal period, use the ANRQ Postnatal version, which includes additional questions about birth and parenting experiences.

An ANRQ score greater than 23 may indicate the need for further discussion and follow-up.

Further assessment should also be considered when there is:

- a significant mental health history
- a history of abuse
- clear signs or risks of distress

The ANRQ has been translated into more than 25 languages.

However, evidence regarding its use in migrant and refugee women is limited, so cultural factors should be considered.

### Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women

The ANRQ was not developed or validated with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representation and may not reflect Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander world views.

A conversational approach that focuses on building rapport and trust may be more appropriate.

The Kimberley Mum's Mood Scale (KMMS) may be a culturally appropriate tool in some Aboriginal communities.

If using the KMMS:

- use the complete tool
- complete both Part 1 and Part 2

### Documentation and follow-up

Document all psychosocial risk factors identified.

Confirm and explore these concerns with the woman.

Explain the assessment results.

Develop an agreed plan for:

- monitoring
- referral
- ongoing support

## Family violence

Family violence may involve partners, siblings, parents, children, carers and other family members.

Intimate partner violence includes behaviour within an intimate relationship that causes physical, psychological or sexual harm, including:

- physical aggression
- psychological abuse
- forced intercourse or other sexual coercion
- controlling behaviours

The postpartum period is a time of increased risk for the onset or escalation of family violence.

Australian evidence suggests that family violence during the first year postpartum affects approximately 5.1% to 17% of women.

Family violence is associated with physical and mental health problems including:

- depression
- anxiety
- post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
- poorer breastfeeding outcomes

### Recommendation status

The recommendations in this Family violence section were approved by the LEAPP Steering Committee on 11 June 2025.

They are draft recommendations and had not yet been approved by NHMRC at the time this guideline was published.

### Training for healthcare providers

Seek and regularly update training in:

- family violence screening
- family violence support services
- culturally safe care

Healthcare providers should be trained to ask sensitive questions, respond appropriately and help women feel safe and supported.

### Screening for family violence

Screen all women during the postpartum period before discharge from hospital or birth centre.

Repeat screening at every postnatal visit for women who:

- are at risk of family violence
- show signs or symptoms of family violence

Screen for family violence face-to-face when the woman is alone.

Screening should occur in a safe and private environment.

If the woman is not alone or does not feel safe, reschedule screening for a more appropriate time.

Where possible, screening should occur within a continuum of care with a trusted healthcare provider.

### Signs that may indicate family violence

Healthcare providers should be alert to signs including:

- physical injury
- emotional distress
- body language
- anxiety in the presence of a partner
- post-traumatic stress disorder
- concerns about the wellbeing or development of children
- other signs of an unsafe family environment

### Before screening

Before conducting family violence screening, discuss mandatory reporting requirements when children are involved.

Explain:

- the limits of confidentiality
- the possible implications of disclosure
- that the aim is to prioritise safety and provide support
- that the woman's autonomy will be respected

### Screening tools

Use a validated or State or Territory-specific tool to screen for family violence.

There is no screening tool validated specifically for postnatal women.

Family violence screening tools used during pregnancy are also commonly used during the postnatal period.

### Responding to disclosure

Provide first-line support to women who disclose family violence.

This should include:

- acknowledging the woman's response
- listening without judgement
- validating her experience
- helping to enhance safety
- supporting safety planning
- providing information about available resources
- linking her with appropriate family violence support services
- supporting choice and control without imposing solutions

The woman's response should be acknowledged and respected whether or not she discloses violence.

Women who do not disclose family violence should still receive information about:

- family violence
- support services
- where to seek help if needed in the future

Broad written information about local support services and helpline numbers may be safer than material that is specifically labelled as family violence information.

### Family violence support services

Healthcare providers should be aware of local family support services and community resources that address:

- family violence
- sexual assault

These services should be accessible for both urgent and ongoing support.

### Cultural and language considerations

Provide culturally safe responses for all women experiencing family violence, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women.

Women from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds may face additional barriers to disclosure and accessing support.

These may include:

- cultural barriers
- safety concerns
- difficulties accessing appropriate translation services

Use only accredited professional interpreters when screening for or discussing family violence.

Do not use:

- partners
- children
- other family members
- friends

as interpreters when discussing family violence.

Responses should align with the woman's needs and community context.

### Privacy and safety

Family violence screening should only occur in a safe and private setting.

Online or telehealth screening may compromise safety if privacy cannot be assured.

During home visits, ensure the woman is alone and in a safe environment before screening.

If this is not possible, arrange another suitable and safe time.

## Bereavement support

Perinatal loss, including termination of pregnancy, miscarriage, stillbirth and neonatal death, can have profound and long-lasting effects on parents and families.

Parents may experience intense grief that can persist for years and may continue into future pregnancies.

Perinatal loss can also be associated with mental health problems including:

- anxiety
- depression
- post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

The quality of care and support provided after perinatal loss is important for the immediate and long-term wellbeing of parents and other family members.

### Recommendation status

The recommendations in this Bereavement support section were approved by the LEAPP Steering Committee on 11 June 2025.

They are draft recommendations and had not yet been approved by NHMRC at the time this guideline was published.


### Communication and decision-making

Use respectful and sensitive language that is honest, realistic and understandable, while taking into account the individual needs of parents.

Take the lead from parents about the language they prefer when referring to their baby.

Use the word "baby" or "bub" if this is acceptable to the parents.

If the baby has been named, ask permission before using the baby's name.

Offer individually tailored information about:

- perinatal grief
- what parents may expect
- decisions that need to be made around the time of the loss

Give parents enough time and a private space to consider the options available to them.

Health professionals should aim to use shared decision-making when discussing difficult topics, including:

- palliative care options
- autopsy
- memory making
- funeral or memorial arrangements

Information should be provided:

- clearly and honestly
- in a language and format suited to the parents' needs
- at different time points where needed
- in manageable amounts, recognising that grief can make information difficult to absorb

Where required, use an interpreter or signer.

Parents should be given uninterrupted time in a private space to process information and discuss choices relating to their baby.


### Memory making

Recognise the loss of the baby, regardless of gestation.

Offer parents multiple opportunities to create memories, while giving them time to reflect and decide what they want.

Health professionals should introduce memory-making options early and provide ongoing opportunities and support.

Possible mementos can include:

- photographs
- handprints and footprints
- casts
- locks of hair
- cot cards
- identification bracelets
- special clothing
- scans and ultrasound images

Memory making should always be optional and guided by the parents' wishes, beliefs and preferences.

Some parents may feel unsure, conflicted or fearful about seeing their baby or creating memories.

Use a supportive and flexible approach, recognising that parents may change their minds over time.


### Emotional and psychological support

Provide information and opportunities for social and emotional support after perinatal loss.

Support options may include:

- peer support
- professional counselling
- psychology services
- other bereavement support services where available

Establish and use referral pathways to ensure appropriate ongoing community-based support.

This may include referral to:

- social workers
- GPs
- community health services
- professional psychological support

Consider professional psychological support particularly for parents who:

- are at risk of mental health problems such as post-traumatic stress
- have pre-existing mental health conditions
- have little or no social support

Partners and other family members may also experience significant grief.

Acknowledge that their grief may be different from the grief experienced by the birthing parent and may be expressed differently.

Avoid making assumptions about how parents will grieve or what type of support they will find helpful.

Support may be needed from the time of the loss through to future pregnancies.


### Discharge planning and follow-up

Follow usual discharge planning processes, including routine midwifery postnatal care in addition to bereavement support.

Ensure that appropriate follow-up appointments are arranged to discuss:

- the circumstances surrounding the loss
- possible reasons for the loss
- any ongoing investigations
- expected timeframes for results

Parents should be kept informed about investigations into the cause of their baby's death.

Comprehensive discharge planning should include:

- immediate emotional support
- practical support
- clear pathways to ongoing community-based care

Bereaved parents may feel unsupported after discharge, which can increase grief and isolation.

### Culturally tailored care

Provide care that is tailored to individual:

- personal needs
- cultural needs
- religious needs
- spiritual needs

Healthcare providers should take time to understand the family's beliefs, values and decision-making preferences.

Bereavement care should be culturally safe and responsive to the individual needs of parents and families.

## Perineal health and healing

Perineal trauma is common after vaginal birth and may include:

- first-degree tears
- second-degree tears
- episiotomy
- third-degree tears
- fourth-degree tears

### Routine postnatal care

At each postnatal contact:

- ask about concerns with perineal wound healing
- offer a perineal examination by a care provider
- assess and monitor perineal pain
- consider using a validated pain scale

Provide information about:

- the type of wound, such as an episiotomy or repaired tear
- expected pain and swelling
- normal progressive wound healing

### Perineal hygiene

Advise women about good perineal hygiene, including:

- showering the perineum daily
- changing sanitary pads regularly
- washing hands before and after perineal care

### Pain management

If a woman reports perineal pain:

- encourage examination
- discuss pain relief options
- provide appropriate analgesia

Be aware that perineal pain that persists or worsens in the first few weeks after birth may be associated with:

- depression
- long-term perineal pain
- difficulty with daily functioning
- psychosexual difficulties

### When urgent assessment is needed

If the perineal wound breaks down or there are ongoing concerns about healing, refer the woman urgently to:

- the nearest maternity service
- a hospital emergency department
- the closest appropriate emergency care provider

The wound should be assessed by a health professional skilled in obstetric and surgical care.

**Recommendation status:** This wound breakdown recommendation was approved by the LEAPP Steering Committee on 11 June 2025 and had not yet been approved by NHMRC at the time this guideline was published.

### Seek immediate help if any of the following occur

- unusual or uncontrolled flatulence
- faecal incontinence
- urinary incontinence
- increasing perineal pain
- fever
- flu-like symptoms
- unpleasant-smelling discharge
- redness
- unusual heat around the wound
- reduced sensation

### Wound infection and breakdown

Possible signs of infection include:

- wound breakdown
- swelling
- redness
- unpleasant-smelling discharge
- pain that worsens or does not resolve

These symptoms require urgent assessment.

### Tampons and sexual activity

Advise women to avoid tampons for 6 weeks after birth to support wound healing.

For women who wish to be sexually active, consider non-penetrative sexual activity for the first 6 weeks after birth to support wound healing.

### Risk factors for persistent perineal pain

Risk factors include:

- episiotomy
- labial or perineal tear
- assisted vaginal birth using forceps or vacuum
- wound infection
- wound breakdown
- birth experienced as traumatic by the woman

### Additional information

Perineal trauma can lead to short-term complications such as:

- wound infection
- wound breakdown

Longer-term complications can include:

- pain during sex
- urinary incontinence
- pelvic organ prolapse
- psychosexual difficulties

Women with repaired perineal wounds may experience soreness until sutures dissolve.

Women should be encouraged to raise concerns about pain or wound healing during postnatal care.

Healthcare providers should consider:

- cultural needs
- language needs
- gender preferences
- whether the woman would like a partner, support person or chaperone present during examination

Women with wound complications should receive timely assessment and management.

## Preeclampsia and hypertension

Hypertensive disorders in pregnancy include:

- gestational hypertension
- preeclampsia
- chronic hypertension
- preeclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension

Postpartum hypertension generally refers to hypertension occurring after birth up to 6 weeks postpartum.

Women may have:

- persistent hypertension after pregnancy
- new hypertension after a previously normal pregnancy

Persistent hypertension is associated with higher rates of emergency department visits and hospital readmissions.

These recommendations are based on the Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand (SOMANZ) Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023.

### NSAIDs for postpartum pain

Do not routinely use non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for postpartum pain management in inpatient women with preeclampsia.

NSAIDs may be considered for short-term inpatient use in selected circumstances where clinically appropriate.

### Antihypertensive medications during breastfeeding

When prescribing antihypertensive medication to breastfeeding women, discuss:

- the benefits of treatment
- the potential risks
- the possibility of medication transfer into breastmilk

Current evidence suggests that medication transfer into breastmilk is generally low for commonly used antihypertensive medications, but individualised decision-making is recommended.

### Loop diuretics

Consider short-term use of loop diuretics for women with postpartum hypertension related to preeclampsia when clinically indicated, such as:

- pulmonary oedema
- clinical signs of fluid overload

### Additional information

Postpartum preeclampsia most commonly develops within 48 hours after birth but can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum or occasionally later.

Risk factors include:

- hypertension during pregnancy
- previous preeclampsia
- previous postpartum preeclampsia
- obesity
- multiple pregnancy
- family history of preeclampsia

Women taking antihypertensive medication while breastfeeding should receive individual counselling balancing:

- benefits of blood pressure control
- benefits of breastfeeding
- potential medication exposure through breastmilk

Commonly used medications including nifedipine, labetalol, metoprolol, propranolol and enalapril are generally transferred into breastmilk in very small amounts.

Monitoring breastfed infants for hypotension, bradycardia or poor feeding may be appropriate if there are concerns about medication effects.

## Postnatal discharge planning

Postnatal discharge refers to the transfer of care of the mother and baby from the place of birth to the home or community setting.

Discharge planning should begin before discharge and involve the woman, family or carers, and relevant healthcare providers.

### Before discharge or transfer

When planning discharge, consider:

- geographical location
- organisational and individual resources
- access to services
- model of care, including continuity of care
- the woman's preferences
- cultural practices and cultural safety

Decide on the timing of discharge in consultation with the woman, recognising that preferences may change.

### Assessment before discharge

Before transfer to community care, discuss and assess:

- the birth experience and any questions
- physical health, including pain
- mental health and emotional wellbeing
- bladder function
- knowledge, skills and confidence to care for herself
- knowledge, skills and confidence to care for the baby
- individual needs and preferences, including cultural practices

Assess the baby's:

- physical health
- signs of deterioration
- urine output
- passage of meconium
- weight
- nutritional status
- feeding plan

Observe at least one effective feed before discharge.

Advise parents to seek medical advice if the baby has not passed meconium within 24 hours of birth.

### Home circumstances

Before discharge, assess factors that may affect care at home, including:

- available community services
- social supports
- the home environment
- the knowledge, skills and confidence of other caregivers

Ensure any required referrals and follow-up appointments have been arranged and provide written information to the family.

If any assessments cannot be completed before discharge, establish a plan for completion after discharge.

### Transfer of care

Ensure clear communication between healthcare providers regarding:

- pregnancy, birth and postnatal history
- ongoing care plans
- outstanding assessments
- previous pregnancy history where relevant
- mental health history and current wellbeing
- baby's feeding
- concerns about the woman or baby
- cultural support requirements where appropriate
- child safety concerns where appropriate

Provide discharge summary documentation to:

- the woman
- other carers where appropriate
- receiving healthcare providers

Ensure the discharge information is understood.

### Information before going home

Provide information about:

- the transfer of care process
- what to expect after birth
- caring for the baby
- ongoing healthcare
- planning future pregnancies
- available government and community support services
- who to contact if concerns arise

Where available, provide written or digital resources appropriate to the family's circumstances, including translated or picture-based resources.

### Ongoing postnatal care

Arrange the first postnatal contact within 24 to 48 hours after transfer to community care.

Where feasible and consistent with the woman's preferences, offer follow-up:

- at home
- in a clinic
- via telehealth

Arrange at least three postnatal contacts.

Spread follow-up contacts across the postnatal period so support is available when most needed without overwhelming the family.

### Additional information

Discharge planning should ideally begin during pregnancy.

Plans should be individualised according to:

- maternal health
- newborn health
- family support
- cultural needs
- geographical access to services
- psychosocial circumstances

Women returning home without their baby, including after perinatal loss or when the baby remains in hospital, require appropriate discharge planning and ongoing support.

Effective discharge education should include:

- self-care
- newborn care
- feeding
- safe sleeping
- where to obtain medical help
- available parenting and community support services

## Infant feeding

### Alcohol while breastfeeding

Advise women not to consume alcohol while breastfeeding to prevent potential harm to the baby.

### If a breastfeeding woman chooses to drink alcohol

Use a supportive, non-judgmental approach.

Discuss practical ways to reduce risk.

Breastmilk expressed and stored before drinking alcohol will not contain alcohol and can be used to feed the baby afterwards.

For an average woman, it takes about 2 hours from the start of drinking for one standard drink of alcohol to clear from breastmilk, although this varies between individuals.

More time is needed for each additional drink.

Breastmilk is free of alcohol only once the woman's blood alcohol level has returned to zero.

Expressing or "pumping and dumping" does not:

- speed up alcohol clearance
- reduce the alcohol concentration in the remaining breastmilk

Expressing may still help maintain milk supply, but milk expressed while alcohol remains in the bloodstream should not be given to the baby.

### Additional information

There is no established safe amount of alcohol during breastfeeding.

Alcohol passes into breastmilk at approximately the same concentration as in the blood.

Newborn babies and young infants may be particularly vulnerable to the effects of alcohol exposure.

Alcohol exposure through breastmilk may:

- affect feeding
- reduce milk flow
- affect infant sleep
- cause sedation
- potentially affect neurodevelopment

Women who find it difficult to stop problematic alcohol use should be offered supportive resources and referral to appropriate services.

Partners, family and friends can support breastfeeding women by reducing or avoiding their own alcohol consumption.
